0.$description: No space — the rung a padding or gap aliases when a variant removes it, so the property stays bound rather than deleted.

2.$description: 2px — hairline separation: a badge from its glyph, a focus ring's offset (`focus/offset`).

4.$description: 4px — the tightest inner gap: icon to label inside a chip, the gap between stacked pills.

8.$description: 8px — the base unit. A control's inner gap (`density/control/gap`), a label to its field, `target/spacing` between adjacent targets.

12.$description: 12px — compact padding: dense table cells and compact controls (`density/control/padding/x` compact).

16.$description: 16px — the default inline padding of a control and the mobile page margin (`grid/margin/mobile`).

20.$description: 20px — card padding at the compact end, and the gap between a card's header and body.

24.$description: 24px — the grid gutter (`grid/gutter`), the tablet page margin, and default card padding.

32.$description: 32px — the desktop-wide page margin (`grid/margin/desktop`) and the inner padding of a section band.

40.$description: 40px — the gap between related blocks inside a section on a portal page.

48.$description: 48px — the default gap between page sections (`section/48`) on the website.

56.$description: 56px — a section gap for a page with a hero above it, so the hero reads as its own band.

64.$description: 64px — the vertical padding of a hero or a login panel gutter (`layout/login/panel/gutter`).

72.$description: 72px — the generous section gap used between website home-page bands.

80.$description: 80px — the widest routine section gap; above this the page reads as separate pages.

120.$description: 120px — the top and bottom inset of a full-bleed hero band.

360.$description: 360px — the fixed inset the login hero's content column sits behind; the one rung that is a layout offset, not a gap.

space.$description: Spacing ladder, VALUE-NAMED: `space/16` is 16px. Renamed from T-shirt labels on 2026-08-18. Two reasons, both measured. (1) A T-shirt ramp has no slot between two adjacent rungs, so every insertion forces a rename of everything above it — that happened twice in one day (inline gained 24, padding needed 6). A numeric ladder absorbs any step for free. (2) The Tier-2 families each mapped the SAME label to a DIFFERENT value — `l` was 16 in inline, 24 in stack, 20 in padding and 56 in section — which is inherited verbatim from UX4G 3.0 and is the single most confusing thing about the old scale. UX4G's own primitive ramp is numeric (space-1..16), so numbering here is MORE consistent with UX4G, not less. UX4G parity is unaffected: the --ux4g-* layer is emitted independently and never reads these names. 6px is new — UX4G ships it as space-3 and 400 padding properties in the Figma library needed it.

radius.$description: Radius ladder — VALUE-NAMED. The rung IS the pixel value, except `full`, a sentinel meaning fully rounded. Tier 1: hidden from publishing, banned in app code.

display.$description: The optical Display cut, for the 40-80px Display ramp. Noto Sans ships two cuts of one design: the text cut is drawn for reading at 12-24px, and at 80px its open spacing reads as loose. The Display cut tightens it. This is now genuinely LOADED (apps/hub root layout, weight 500) — for a long time it was named here and loaded nowhere, so it fell through to the text cut and the matching Figma variable could not resolve at all. LATIN ONLY: `Noto Sans Display` has no Devanagari subset and `Noto Sans Devanagari` has no Display cut, so a Hindi heading falls through to Noto Sans by design. In Figma the same cut is a STYLE of Noto Sans ("Display Medium"), not a family — see design.md.
display.$value: "Noto Sans Display", "Noto Sans", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif

mono.$description: CODE AND TECHNICAL STRINGS ONLY — token names, CSS snippets, file paths in the design-system docs. NOT for numbers, amounts or reference numbers: those want `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on Noto Sans, which aligns digits down a column while keeping them in the same typeface as the text beside them. Switching a data column to a monospace face is the clumsier fix and looks like a different design. The estate already does this correctly in the Aadhaar/PAN field, the charts, the SLA indicator and the shared DataTable. DELIBERATELY a system stack: `ui-monospace` resolves to the platform's own mono (SF Mono, Cascadia, Roboto Mono) — all well-drawn, all disambiguating 0/O and 1/l/I, and already on the device. A webfont here would download on every page to style sample code on a handful of documentation pages, which on a low-bandwidth government audience is not a trade worth making. IBM Plex Mono was set here briefly and reverted for that reason.
mono.$value: ui-monospace, "Cascadia Code", "Source Code Pro", Menlo, monospace

icon.$description: The ICON face — Material Symbols Rounded, the official SAMAVESH icon system. It is here for the same reason every other family is: a Material Symbols glyph is TEXT, not artwork, so its family is a typographic decision the design system owns rather than a constant three files happen to agree on. Before this token the name was a literal in `icons.css` (twice) and in all seven Figma `Icon/*` text styles, which is four places to change and no way to prove they still match. The stack is the family plus a generic, so a failed webfont falls back to a real face rather than to nothing; Figma takes only the first entry (`primaryFontFamily`), which is exactly the family name its picker resolves. NOT a Tier-2 role — bind `font/icon` from anything that renders.

lineHeight.$description: Leading is a property of a role, not a primitive: every type/<role>/lh is authored beside its size. The one thing here is the Devanagari OFFSET the build derives each role's lhDevanagari from. The numeric flat ramp (font.lineHeight.16…56) that used to sit beside it was retired 2026-09-04, and the flat unitless 1.7 that followed it on the same day — one line height for every Hindi block, which undid the scale and which Figma read as 1.7px.

devanagariOffset.$description: Extra leading Devanagari takes over the same role's Latin leading, as a fraction of the size: the script hangs from the शिरोरेखा and stacks vowel signs above and below, so it needs a fixed share of its size in extra vertical room at any size — not a different rhythm. lhDevanagari = lh + 0.2 × size, rounded UP to the 4px grid: body-1 16/24 → 28, headline-1 40/48 → 56, display-1 80/88 → 104. A ratio, not a length: never bind it in Figma — bind the role's lhDevanagari.

role.$description: Two-surface responsive type role scale (Portal DS naming: hyphenated roles). Each size/lh/para carries mosje.type website/portal min+max bounds (min at 360px viewport, max at 1280px). The formatter emits --sa-type-ROLE-size/lh/para as clamp(min, fluid, max): Website in :root, Portal under data-surface=portal. $value is the Website desktop fallback. RE-CUT 2026-09-04: Title, Body and Label are IDENTICAL on both surfaces (the productive core is shared, as Carbon's productive set is), only Display and Headline differ by surface; every size is on the 16-step ramp 12·14·16·18·20·22·24·28·32·36·40·48·56·64·72·80 (36 is DBIM §4's desktop H1, UX4G's Display/XS, and the phone bound of display-2), every line height on the 4px grid, leading ratios rise monotonically as size falls (display 1.10→1.20, headline 1.20→1.50), body is 1.5 on both surfaces, and nothing renders below 12px (UX4G 3.0 §2 minimum; label-3 is the CAPS role at 12/16 with type/caps/tracking). The 13px and 15px stops the old Portal ramp carried are gone.

tracking.$description: Letter-spacing (Portal DS naming). Display tiers carry negative tracking on BOTH surfaces, derived from one em rule per rung (display-1/2 −0.015em, 3/4 −0.01em, 5 −0.005em, 6 zero) against each surface's own size bounds, so the two surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Heading, title, body and label are zero: Noto Sans is drawn with the spacing they need. `caps` is the one positive value, for the 12px uppercase label role. mosje.type website/portal min+max (px).

1.$description: Display-1 letter-spacing, −0.015em of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

2.$description: Display-2 letter-spacing, −0.015em of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

3.$description: Display-3 letter-spacing, −0.01em of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

4.$description: Display-4 letter-spacing, −0.01em of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

5.$description: Display-5 letter-spacing, −0.005em of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

6.$description: Display-6 letter-spacing, 0 of the size at each bound, so the website and portal surfaces track alike per pixel of type. Large Noto Sans Display sets slightly tight; below display-6 the drawn spacing is right and tracking is zero.

heading.$description: Headline tier tracking: zero. Noto Sans at 16–40px is drawn with the spacing a heading needs; negative tracking here closes counters and hurts Devanagari.

body.$description: Body tracking: zero. Positive tracking on running text lowers reading speed; WCAG 1.4.12 requires the reader's own override to survive, which zero tracking makes trivial.

label.$description: Label tracking: zero for mixed-case labels. Uppercase labels are the label-3 role and take type/caps/tracking instead.

caps.$description: Tracking for the CAPS label role (label-3, 12px, uppercase): +0.06em, which at 12px is 0.72px. The only positive tracking in the system; uppercase without it is a defect the type gate reports.

font.$description: Tier 1 typography: the families by script (latin, devanagari, display, mono, icon), the Devanagari leading offset, the 21 type roles (display · headline · title · body · label, each with size, line height and paragraph spacing, fluid between the website and portal surfaces) and the tracking per tier. Emitted as the Tier-2 --sa-type-* scale; bind a role's text style, never a raw step.

shadow.$description: Tier 1 elevation ramp as DTCG composite shadows (an array of layers, each carrying color, offsetX, offsetY, blur and spread), so a layer can be read by the Figma effect-style writer and the docs without parsing CSS. none→xl is a 6-level superset of UX4G 3.0's 5-level l0…l4, tinted toward ink rather than UX4G's flat black — tinted shadows read as depth instead of dirt on a light government surface. The ink is GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs from neutral/800 — the body ink these are tinted toward — so it cannot drift from it again. Geometry stays authored here; only the rgb is derived.

none.$description: No effect. Bind it deliberately to reset an elevation something else applied. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

xs.$description: One tight layer at 12% — a card resting on the page. Enough to separate, not enough to float. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

sm.$description: Two layers, 10% + 6% — a surface lifted on interaction. The second layer is the contact shadow that stops the lift reading as a cut-out. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

md.$description: Two layers, 9% + 5% — a menu or popover. Larger offset, lower alpha: higher surfaces cast softer, wider shadows. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

lg.$description: Two layers, 8% + 3% — a dialog. Softest per-layer alpha in the ramp; the scrim behind it does the suppressing. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

xl.$description: One wide layer at 18% — a toast. Heavier than lg on purpose: it arrives unannounced and has to be found without a scrim. Colour is neutral/800 (the body ink) at the stated alpha, retinted by build/brand-ramps.mjs; geometry is authored here.

inset.$description: The one INSET shadow — a shallow well, 1px down and 2px of blur at 8% ink, drawn inside the surface. For a pressed well, an inset track, a field that reads as a recess. Retinted per brand like every other shadow layer.

motion.$description: Tier 1 motion primitives: a value-named duration ladder and five named easing curves. Value-named like space and radius, so a rung's name IS its value (Polaris names durations the same way). Nothing in app code binds these — bind a motion/<intent> pair, which carries the duration AND the easing that belongs to it.

duration.$description: Milliseconds. 0 is the reduced-motion floor and the instant intent; 50–150 is direct feedback (a press, a hover, a colour change) — the band Material 3 calls short; 200–300 is something arriving, leaving or resizing — medium; 400–500 is a deliberate, attention-carrying move — long; 700 is the ceiling, for a full-page or skeleton fade. Anything longer reads as lag on a government form.

easing.$description: Named by BEHAVIOUR, following Material 3's vocabulary, so a designer and a developer say the same word: decelerate for things arriving, accelerate for things leaving, standard for a move the reader watches, emphasized for a surface the reader opened, linear for progress and spinners only. The curves are the same four the estate shipped since 2026-06 plus linear; only the names moved (out → decelerate, in → accelerate, inOut → standard, outStrong → emphasized).

linear.$description: Constant rate. Progress bars, spinners and anything that measures time. Never for an element that moves — a linear move reads as mechanical.

accelerate.$description: Starts slow, leaves fast. Things LEAVING the screen: they get out of the way and the eye does not follow them out. Material 3 standard-accelerate.

decelerate.$description: Arrives fast, settles gently. Things ENTERING the screen and any colour, border or shadow change on hover — the change is over before the reader looks for it. Material 3 standard-decelerate.

standard.$description: Eases at both ends. A move the reader is meant to watch — an element changing place or size on the same screen. Material 3 standard.

emphasized.$description: Exponential ease-out. Most of the distance is covered in the first third, so a large surface reads as arriving under its own momentum rather than being played back at a fixed rate. For anything the reader opened — a drawer, a panel, a disclosure — and for press feedback.

border.$description: Border widths. UX4G 3.0's exact values (border-none/thin/thick/thicker/thickest), bound by name so the two cannot drift — spec §8.1 'structural' rule.

width.$description: Tier 1 stroke widths in px. The group carries its own $type because Style Dictionary merges this tree with the semantic `border` colour roles — the nearest ancestor wins, and a width must never inherit `color`.

opacity.$description: Opacity scale — thirteen steps, ONE ladder, derived from what the estate's translucent tokens use plus the two roles it will foreseeably need: 0 (transparent), 4 (hairline and faint lift on a dark surface), 8–48 in eights (the six wash and overlay tiers), 64 and 72 (disabled and secondary ink on a dark surface), 80 and 88 (pressed and hover fill of an inverse button), 100 (opaque). Rationalised 2026-09-04 from UX4G 3.0's fourteen steps plus ten estate one-offs: 5, 20, 25, 60, 75, 90 had zero consumers anywhere in the estate; 3, 10, 30, 45, 50, 70, 84, 92 each served one or two tokens and now sit on the ladder (3→4, 10→8, 30→32, 45→48, 50→48, 70→72, 84→80, 92→88). The UX4G parity stylesheet carries UX4G's own values as literals, so nothing UX4G publishes is lost; the divergence is recorded in docs/audit/2026-09-04-colour-system-audit-and-redesign.md §16. Consumers bind the Tier-2 `alpha/*` aliases, never this scale.

size.$description: One numeric size scale, VALUE-NAMED: `size/16` is 16px. Adopted from UX4G 3.0, whose 20 steps are carried at their exact rem values — the name needing no lookup is the thing worth copying, and it is what Tailwind and Spectrum do too. 22 and 44 are a SAMAVESH superset: our type scale already ships them and UX4G has no step there.

breakpoint.$description: Viewport anchors. These are not decoration: `clamp()` interpolates type between mobile and desktop, and Figma's Type modes sample the same curve at all three. The numbers were duplicated as literals in two build files until 2026-08-10 — this is now their one source.

mobile.$description: The narrowest width the estate designs for. Every page is built here first (mobile-first) and only gains columns above it.

tablet.$description: Where the page margin steps from 16 to 24 and two-column layouts become possible.

laptop.$description: The third anchor, and the one the ladder was missing. Between tablet (768) and desktop (1280) sat a 512px void with no token in it — which is where iPad landscape, 11-13" laptops and every half-screen window on a 2K monitor live. Anything needing to change at 1024 had to hardcode it or round to one of the neighbours. Matches Tailwind's `lg`, so the token and the utility variant used across this estate finally agree. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md.

desktop.$description: Where the sidebar and content sit side by side and the page cap of 1200 engages.

desktopXl.$description: Where the content cap widens from `container/content` (1200) to `container/contentXl` (1320). 1768 -> 1600 -> 1440 over 2026-08-24, each step decided by measuring the page rather than by citing a ladder. 1768 was abandoned because a 1728-wide viewport carried 264px of margin each side against 1768's own 224px — margins NARROWING as the screen grew. 1600 (Material 3's extra-large window class) was then abandoned because it left the ladder's WEAKEST POINT sitting on its most common viewport: at 1536 — 1920 at 125% Windows scaling, the single most common desktop width — content held only 75% of the screen, worse than at 1280 (90%) and worse than at 1600 (78%). 1440 fixes the range that carries the most users: 1440 goes 80% -> 88%, 1512 76% -> 84%, 1536 75% -> 83%. Nothing at 1600 and above changes. THE FLOOR THAT WAS DROPPED, deliberately: earlier notes held that 1440 must stay on the 1200 cap because UX4G says '1200px desktop'. UX4G publishes no breakpoints at all, so it never fixed where desktop ends; and `.claude/rules/standards-precedence.md` puts interface quality above it, which is the whole point of that rule. Recorded as divergence #6 in docs/guidelines/README.md. It also makes the code agree with the Handoff, whose Home frame draws a 1320 container on a 1440 artboard — the frame was right and the note calling it wrong has been withdrawn. Not part of the type curve — `clamp()` still tops out at 1280, so this anchor resizes no glyph.

desktopWide.$description: The fifth anchor, where the cap widens a second time to `container/contentWide` (1440). Without it a 2560-wide monitor rendered a 1320 column between 620px margins — 48% of the screen given to nothing, which is the complaint that started this. One step is not enough for the range 1600-2560+: a single cap either starves the desktop or sprawls on the monitor. Stops at 1440 rather than continuing to grow because beyond that a 12-column grid starts costing more in eye travel than it returns in density. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md.
